newsitem.title: JAPAN: "Bubble" debt bites deep at Japan sushi chain.
newsitem.headline: "Bubble" debt bites deep at Japan sushi chain.

text.p: A chain of sushi restaurants said on Monday it had sought protection from creditors under Japan's bankruptcy laws, becoming the latest corporate casualty of the nation's "bubble" era excesses.
Kyotaru Co Ltd, said it made the insolvency filing on Sunday at a Tokyo court with debts of some $865 million.
Kyotaru is the first firm listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange to fail since mid-1993.

"The scars of the bubble economy are evident in the finance sector but Kyotaru was a surprise," a stock trader at a foreign brokerage said. "The aftermath of the bubble may be a lot more serious than it seems."
Analysts said the scale of Japanese corporate bankruptcies remained high and the outlook bleak as the nation's huge economy struggles to achieve solid recovery.
They said there would be no early respite from the high level of business failures, with signs that the economy may slip back into a slump after a planned sales tax rise in April.
Kyotaru's business failure was taken as suggesting that Japan Inc was still in trouble and prompted active sales of Japanese shares in hectic trading on Monday.
On the Tokyo stock market, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares ended down 609.70 points, or 3.37 percent, at 17,480.34. At one stage it fell over 850 points to 17,237.27.
Kyotaru buckled under the weight of debts resulting from rapid domestic expansion and investment in the United States during Japan's 1980s bubble of soaring asset prices and unbridled consumption.

After hitting a peak in 1991 with annual sales of 82.49 billion yen ($705 million), the firm's business has deteriorated amid losses from hefty real estate holdings and financial trouble at one of its affiliates, Kyotaru Shoji Co.
In 1993, the company adopted a three-year business restructuring plan, closing down its unprofitable chain stores and restaurants, but the efforts failed to bear fruit.

Kyotaru, which offers take-out sushi and runs sushi restaurants, was also hard hit by a food poisoning epidemic that swept Japan last year and made customers wary of eating uncooked food. The worsened relations with its main bank, Fuji Bank Ltd, also made its restructuring difficult.

Under the filing at Tokyo District Court, Kyotaru will seek to restructure and to salvage parts of its business under court protection. The company said its debts totalled 101.3 billion yen ($865 million), far exceeding its assets of 62.26 billion yen ($532 million).
Kyotaru, set up in 1950 and employing over 1,800 people, plans to strive for "business as usual" while streamlining operations at inefficient restaurants and divisions.

Under Japan's Corporate Rehabilitation Law, the assets of a financially strapped company are protected from creditors by the court if the court decides to proceed with the firm's request for restructuring.

Kyotaru shares were placed under surveillance on Monday -- a formal procedure in which dealing authorities signal caution about particular shares -- before being delisted from the exchange on April 20.
The last failure of a firm from the bourse's main section was Nikkatsu Corp in July 1993. The movie company went bust with debts of about 50 billion yen ($427 million).

The legacy of debt and bad loans left by the collapse of the economic bubble in the early 1990s is still pushing many troubled companies to the wall, even though the economy as a whole has shown signs of stirring back to life.
Recent big business failures include loan firms Nichiei Finance and All Corp as well as realtor Sueno Kosan and major Japanese jeweller Coco Yamaoka Hoshokuten. ($1=117 yen)
